passages.text: This is what Peter gives you under a promise of making you sound-minded. For under the pretext of one God he seems to free you from many lifeless idols. These do not do their worshipers much harm, because with their very eyes they can see that they are stone, bronze, gold, or some other lifeless material. Therefore, knowing that what is seen is nothing, the soul cannot be haunted by fear in the same way through the visible thing. But when, through deceptive teaching, it looks toward a fearsome God, it is uprooted from its natural condition. I say these things not because I advise you to revere idols, but because Peter, while seeming to free your souls from fearsome images, makes each of your minds possessed by a more fearsome image, introducing a God with a form—and, moreover, supremely just. With this comes terror, and shuddering for the soul that thinks of it, capable even of loosening the tension of sound reasoning. For the mind, placed in such a storm, has its brightness muddied like deep water by a violent wind. Therefore, if he comes for your benefit, let him not, while seeming to dissolve your relatively mild fears arising from lifeless forms, introduce in their place a fearsome form of God. But does God have a form? If he does, he has a shape. If he has a shape, how is he not bounded? If bounded, he is in a place. If in a place, he is less than the place containing him. If less than something, how is he greater, stronger, or higher than all? So much for these matters.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς φοβερὸν θεὸν ἀποβλέπουσα τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ἐκβαθρεύεται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: when ... it looks toward a fearsome God, it is uprooted from its natural condition
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the upheaval/derangement image and the author’s contrast with nature; this remains Simon’s reported position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὀρθῶν λογισμῶν ἐκλῦσαι τοὺς τόνους
lexical_decisions.chosen: loosening the tension of sound reasoning
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the tension image rather than merely saying it makes thinking difficult.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μορφὴν δὲ ἔχει θεός;
lexical_decisions.chosen: form ... shape ... bounded
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps distinct vocabulary in the chain of argument. Bounded denotes spatial delimitation, not simply weakness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φοβερῶν ἰδεῶν δοκῶν ἀπαλλάσσειν ὑμῶν τὰς ψυχάς, φοβερωτέρᾳ ἰδέᾳ τὸν ἑκάστου ὑμῶν ἐνθουσιᾶν ποιεῖ νοῦν
lexical_decisions.chosen: while seeming to free your souls from fearsome images, makes each of your minds possessed by a more fearsome image
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰδέα can denote form, appearance, or a mental representation. Images preserves the visual thread through idols, imagined forms, and God in a form without asserting that every image is a physical statue. Ideas or conceptions is a material cognitive alternative but would conceal the unqualified visual sense in modern English.

passages.text: It is also obvious that he does not truly believe even the things said by his own teacher, for he proclaims the opposite of them. For, as I learn, his teacher said to someone, “Do not call me good, for the good one is one.” But when he says “good,” he no longer means that just one whom the scriptures proclaim, who kills and gives life—kills those who sin and gives life to those who live according to his judgment. That he really did not call the maker good is clear to anyone able to think it through. For the maker was known to Adam, whom he formed; to Enoch, who pleased him; to Noah, whom he saw to be righteous; likewise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and also to Moses, the people, and the whole world. Yet Peter’s teacher Jesus came and said, “No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father, and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” Therefore, if the one present was himself the Son, from his coming he revealed to those he wished the one unknown to all. Thus the Father was unknown to everyone before him, not being this one who was known to all.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μή με λέγε ἀγαθόν, ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς εἷς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Do not call me good, for the good one is one
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the wording actually quoted here, not a familiar expanded Gospel form. Simon’s distinction between good and just is retained as his argument.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δημιουργοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the maker
lexical_decisions.rationale: δημιουργός denotes creator or maker, not automatically an evil demiurge; the speaker’s proposed distinction is not editorially endorsed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δικαίῳ ὁραθέντι Νῶε
lexical_decisions.chosen: to Noah, whom he saw to be righteous
lexical_decisions.rationale: δικαίῳ is taken predicatively, righteous being what God perceived in Noah, fitting the list of people pleasing or accepted by the maker. To righteous Noah, whom he saw is the material attributive alternative: righteousness is then Noah’s epithet rather than the content of the seeing. Both retain Noah as the person seen by God; neither reverses the action into Noah seeing God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα, εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός, ὡς οὐδὲ τὸν υἱόν τις οἶδεν εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the distinct Greek knew/knows forms instead of homogenizing the quoted tenses.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀγαθὸν δὲ εἰπὼν οὐκέτι ἐκεῖνον λέγει τὸν δίκαιον
lexical_decisions.chosen: But when he says “good,” he no longer means that just one
lexical_decisions.rationale: No longer retains the additional οὐκέτι force. It can express the logical consequence under the good designation—no longer under that description—rather than necessarily a chronological change of belief. The clause remains Simon’s argument, not a narrator’s endorsement.

passages.text: And in saying this, Jesus does not even agree with himself. For sometimes, in other statements drawn from the scriptures, he establishes a fearsome and just God, saying, “Do not fear the one who kills the body but can do nothing to the soul. Fear the one who can cast both body and soul into the Gehenna of fire. Yes, I tell you, fear this one.” That he really said to fear this one as a just God, to whom he also says the wronged should cry out, is shown when he gives a parable on this and adds its explanation, saying, “If, then, the unjust judge acted in this way because he was petitioned repeatedly, how much more will the Father bring vindication for those who cry to him day and night? Or do you think that because he is patient with them, he will not do it? Yes, I tell you, he will do it, and quickly.” But whoever says that God vindicates and repays establishes him as just by nature, and not good. Further, he also gives thanks to the Lord of heaven and earth. If he is Lord of heaven and earth, he is acknowledged as maker; and being maker, he is just. Calling him good at one time and just at another, he does not agree even in this way. Thirdly, his wise disciple insisted yesterday that direct perception is more adequate than an apparition, not knowing that direct perception can be human, whereas an apparition is acknowledged to belong to divinity.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν γέενναν τοῦ πυρὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Gehenna of fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the named place and fire qualification, not the distinct Hades term.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἐκδίκησιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: vindication
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκδίκησις can be vengeance or the securing of justice. Vindication fits the wronged petitioners while retaining the punitive repayment explained afterward.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνάργειαν ὀπτασίας ἱκανωτέραν εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: direct perception is more adequate than an apparition
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνάργεια here is direct evident encounter, contrasted with ὀπτασία, an apparition. The polemical wise disciple is not softened into neutral description.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνίοτε γὰρ ἄλλαις φωναῖς τῶν ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν φοβερὸν καὶ δίκαιον συνίστησι θεὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For sometimes, in other statements drawn from the scriptures, he establishes a fearsome and just God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes τῶν ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν partitively, other statements among those derived from scripture. The subsequent fear, judgment, and Lord-of-heaven-and-earth material continues Simon’s contrast with the scriptural just maker, favoring this reading. The comparative-genitive alternative is with statements different from those from the scriptures; that would distinguish rather than include the statements’ scriptural derivation. The supplied wording permits both and is not emended.

passages.text: “By these and similar statements, Peter, Simon, standing outside and speaking to the crowds, seems to me to be disturbing most of them. So go out immediately and dissolve his false arguments by the power of truth.” After Zacchaeus said this, Peter prayed as usual and went out. He stood in the place of the previous day, greeted the crowds in the customary manner of reverence toward God, and began to speak as follows: “Our Lord Jesus, being a true prophet—as I will also give assurance about this at the proper time—made concise declarations about matters important to the truth, for these two reasons. First, he addressed people who revered God and knew to believe what he uttered as a declaration, for what was said was not foreign to their customary practice. Second, because he had a limited time to proclaim, he did not employ demonstrative argument, so that he might not spend all his allotted time on arguments. Otherwise he would have been occupied with explaining a few statements that could be understood through effort of soul, and would thus not have presented the arguments important to truth more extensively. For he declared what he wished as to a people able to understand, among whom we too belong. Whenever, on a rare occasion, we did not understand something he said, we asked him privately, so that none of what he said would remain unintelligible to us.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν πρὸ μιᾶς τόπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the place of the previous day
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elliptical before one refers to one day before; no new location is invented.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ τῆς ἀποδείξεως οὐκ ἐχρῆτο λόγῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: he did not employ demonstrative argument
lexical_decisions.rationale: Distinguishes concise pronouncement from developed proof, not truthful from untruthful speech.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὑπὸ πόνου ψυχῆς νοεῖσθαι δυναμένων
lexical_decisions.chosen: that could be understood through effort of soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the intellectual effort supplied by the source rather than rendering the matters permanently incomprehensible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς ἀληθείᾳ διαφέροντας μὴ ἐπὶ πλεῖον εἰσφέρειν λόγους
lexical_decisions.chosen: would thus not have presented the arguments important to truth more extensively
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγους expressly denotes arguments or discourses presented, distinguished from the earlier matters about which declarations were made. Presented retains introducing them into discussion, not simply naming their topics.

passages.text: Knowing, then, that we knew everything he had said and could supply the proofs, when he sent us to the uninstructed nations to baptize them for forgiveness of sins, he commanded us to teach them first. Of these commands, this is the first and great one: to fear the Lord God and serve him alone. The God he said to fear is the one whose angels belonging to the least of the believers among us stand in heaven continually beholding the Father’s face. For he has a form for the sake of primary and sole beauty, and all his members, not for use. He does not have eyes in order to see from there, for he sees from every side, being in body incomparably brighter than the seeing spirit within us and more radiant than every light, so that compared with him the sun’s light is reckoned darkness. Nor does he have ears in order to hear, for from every side he hears, understands, moves, acts, and makes. He has the most beautiful form for the human being’s sake, so that the pure in heart may be able to see him and rejoice in that for which they endured these things. For with his form, as with a most magnificent seal, he stamped out the human being, so that the human being might rule and have dominion over all and everything might serve him. Therefore, judging him to be the whole and the human being his image—he himself invisible, but his image, the human being, visible—the one who wishes to revere him honors his visible image, namely the human being. Whatever someone does to a human being, whether good or evil, is referred to him. Therefore judgment from him will go forth to all, assigning to each what is deserved, for it vindicates his form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μορφὴν γὰρ ἔχει διὰ πρῶτον καὶ μόνον κάλλος
lexical_decisions.chosen: he has a form for the sake of primary and sole beauty
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the unusual first/only qualification of beauty. For beauty first and alone is another possible grouping, treating first adverbially; neither reading makes the form a merely metaphorical appearance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λαμπρότερος ὢν τὸ σῶμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: being in body ... brighter
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the author’s explicit bodily attribution to God without conforming it to a later account of divine incorporeality.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ γὰρ αὐτοῦ μορφῇ ὡς ἐν μεγίστῃ σφραγῖδι τὸν ἄνθρωπον διετυπώσατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: with his form, as with a most magnificent seal, he stamped out the human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the form/seal/imprint sequence and its relation to human dominion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κρίνας εἶναι τὸ πᾶν αὐτὸν καὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ εἰκόνα τὸν ἄνθρωπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: judging him to be the whole and the human being his image
lexical_decisions.rationale: Attaches κρίνας to the following worshipper, whoever wishes to revere him. The worshipper judges God, not himself, to be the whole. Continuing God as subject of a determination from the preceding sentence is a possible contextual alternative: God determined himself to be the whole and the human being his image. The main text chooses the more direct attachment to the following grammatical subject, avoiding a dangling divine determination. The precise God/whole relation is left at the source’s abstract wording, without a later metaphysical explanation.
